113	\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
114	\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
115	\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
116	draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
117	\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
118	one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
119	\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
120	different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
121	and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
122	parameter type ranges over its instances.
123	Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
124	bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
125	taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
126	are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
127	(\chapref{type-inference}).
128	The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
129	parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
130	compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
131	been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
132	A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
133	static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
134	Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
135	every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
136	static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
137	instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
138	shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.

191	by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the

193	dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely

205	that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
206	specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
207	applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696

315	\section{Comprehensions}
316	\seclabel{comprehensions}
317	
318	\note{Array comprehensions are not yet supported.
319	
320	Array comprehensions do not have to be comprehensive --
321	may not define a value for every cell.
322	When an unitialized array cell is accessed, an uncaught exception is raised.}
323	
324	\begin{Grammar}
325	\emph{Comprehension}
326	&::=&
327	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \texttt{[} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
328	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause}$^+$ \texttt{]}\\
329	&$|$&
330	\option{\KWD{BIG}} \{ \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
331	\emph{Entry} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \} \\
332	&$|$& \option{\KWD{BIG}} \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
333	\emph{Expr} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \emph{RightEncloser} \\
334	
335	\emph{Entry} &::=& \emph{Expr} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr} \\
336	
337	\emph{ArrayComprehensionClause} &::=&
338	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} \texttt{|} \emph{GeneratorClauseList}\\
339	
340	\emph{ArrayComprehensionLeft} &::=&
341	\emph{IdOrInt} \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
342	&$|$& \texttt( \emph{IdOrInt}\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrIntList} \texttt) \ensuremath{\mapsto} \emph{Expr}\\
343	
344	\emph{IdOrInt} &::=& \emph{Id}\\
345	&$|$& \emph{IntLiteralExpr}\\
346	
347	\emph{IdOrIntList} &::=& \emph{IdOrInt}(\EXP{,} \emph{IdOrInt})$^*$ \\
348	\end{Grammar}
349	
350	Fortress provides \emph{comprehension} syntax, in which a generator clause list
351	binds values used in the body expression on the left-hand side of the
352	token \EXP{|}.  As described in \secref{generators}, each iteration of
353	the body expression must be assumed to execute in its own implicit
354	thread.  Comprehensions evaluate to aggregate values and have
355	corresponding aggregate types.  The rules for evaluation of a
356	comprehension are similar to those for a reduction expression (see
357	\secref{reduction-expr}).
358	
359	The relationship between a comprehension and an aggregate expression (\secref{aggregate-expr}) is similar to the relationship between a reduction expression (\secref{reduction-expr}) and the corresponding infix operator application (\secref{operator-app-expr}).  The language does not enforce an explicit connection between comprehension syntax and the corresponding aggregate syntax, but in practice libraries that provide definitions for aggregate expressions are expected to define a corresponding comprehension and \emph{vice versa}.  As with reduction expressions, a comprehension using a particular set of enclosers corresponds to a call to a \emph{big bracketing operator}.  Thus the definition of set comprehensions is given by a function with the following signature:
360	%% opr BIG {[\T\] g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0}: Set[\T\]
361	\begin{Fortress}
362	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}} \{\llbracket{}T\rrbracket g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0}\}\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
363	\end{Fortress}
364	This is almost identical to the signature required to define a reduction
365	expression \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}}, shown in \secref{reduction-expr}.
366	Further information on defining comprehensions are described
367	in \secref{defining-generators}.
368	
369	A set comprehension is enclosed in braces, with a left-hand body
370	separated by the token \EXP{|} from a generator clause list.
371	For example, the comprehension:
372	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.SetComp.tex}
373	evaluates to the set
374	\begin{Fortress}
375	\(\{0, 4, 16\}\)
376	\end{Fortress}
377	
378	Map comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
379	except that the left-hand body must be of the form
380	\EXP{e_{1} \mapsto e_{2}}.
381	If \EXP{e_{1}} produces the same value but \EXP{e_{2}} a different value on more
382	than one iteration of the generator list,
383	a \TYP{KeyOverlap} exception is thrown.
384	For example:
385	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.MapComp.tex}
386	evaluates to the map
387	\begin{Fortress}
388	\(\{0 \mapsto 0, 4 \mapsto 8, 16 \mapsto 64\}\)
389	\end{Fortress}
390	
391	
392	List comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
393	except that they are syntactically enclosed in angle brackets.
394	For example:
395	\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.ListComp.tex}
396	evaluates to the list
397	\begin{Fortress}
398	\(\langle 0, 4, 16 \rangle\)
399	\end{Fortress}
400	Note that the order of elements in the resulting list corresponds to
401	the \emph{natural order} of the generators in the generator clause
402	list (see \secref{defining-generators}).
403	
404	Array comprehensions are like set comprehensions, except that they are
405	syntactically enclosed in brackets, and the left-hand body must be of
406	the form \txt{($\mathit{index}_1$, $\mathit{index}_2$, \ldots,
407	  $\mathit{index}_n$) $\mapsto$ $\mathit{e}$}.  Moreover an array
408	comprehension may have multiple clauses separated by semicolons or
409	line breaks.  Each clause conceptually corresponds to an independent loop.
410	Clauses are run in order.  The result is an $n$-dimensional array.
411	For example:
412	\begin{Fortress}
413	\(a = [\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\((x,y,1) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}\)\\
414	\(      (1,y,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid y \gets 1\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
415	\(      (x,1,z) \mapsto 0.0   \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\)\\
416	\(      (x,y,z) \mapsto x+y\cdot z \mid x \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{xSize}, y \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{ySize}, z \gets 2\COLONOP\VAR{zSize}\,]\)\-\\\poptabs
417	\end{Fortress}

   and NonPrimitive.java; the factory name is enshrined in
   WellKnownNames.java.  There must be some factory, named in this

__builtinFactory1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]():Array1[\T,b0,s0\] = do
    r = array1[\T,s0\]()
    typecase N[\b0\] of
        N[\0\] => r
        else => r.subarray[\b0,s0,0\](1)
    end
  end

(* immutableFactory1 is a non-overloaded 0-parameter factory for
   0-indexed 1-D arrays.  It is also mentioned in WellKnownNames as it
   is used to allocate storage for varargs. *)
__immutableFactory1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]():ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\] = do
    r = immutableArray1[\T,s0\]()
    typecase N[\b0\] of
        N[\0\] => r
        else => r.subarray[\b0,s0,0\](1)
    end
  end

__thrower[\T\](): T = throw ForbiddenException(CallerViolation)

(* TODO: fix when Number is covariant. *)

    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> Number => vector[\T,s0\]()
        else => PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]()

array1[\T, nat s0\](v:T):Array1[\T,0,s0\] = array1[\T,s0\]().fill(v)

immutableArray1[\T, nat s0\](): ImmutableArray1[\T,0,s0\] =
    PrimImmutableArray[\T,s0\]()

(* vector is the same as array1, but specialized to numeric type arguments *)

vector[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\](v:T):Vector[\T,s0\] =
    vector[\T,s0\]().fill(v)
tabulatedVector[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\](f:ZZ32->T):Vector[\T,s0\] =
    vector[\T,s0\]().tabulate(f)

pmul[\ T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat k \]
    (a : Vector[\T,k\], b : Vector[\T,k\]):Vector[\T,k\] = a.pmul(b)

opr DOT[\ T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n \]
       (me : Vector[\T,n\], other : Vector[\T,n\]):T = me.dot(other)

# Checker bound defects: rows 680 and 685 to 690 traced, with a fix for each (climb batch 15 probe)

problem: six compiled-checker defects, five distance sites and one crash row. Climb batch 14's record kept them out until they were traced (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-14.md` section 4, "Kept out for want of a measurement"; F-94). Rows 680, 685, 686, 687, 689 and 690.
base: `main` at 873d65f0c. A base build was made at `/home/user/fortress-b15probe-base`, and a worktree was seeded from it. Both were removed after the run.
measured: the distance stage, run once with all three fixes in place: 54 sites became 49. The compiler, othercompiler and library tracks were run twice, once with the minimal fixes and once with the sibling fix added.
committed: `patches/`, `repro/` and `mini-distance.sh` beside this note (`32269d57d`). Nothing in the original tree was committed.

## 1. The answer, row by row

| row | sites | the cause, traced to the line (at 873d65f0c) | the fix (`patches/`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 686 | 1 (`squaredNorm(me)`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2493`) | `TypeAnalyzer.normConjunct` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:692-698`) replaces the closed trait `K` by its listed types that the conjunct `R[\$T\]` does not exclude. The bound then becomes the union `OR(AND(T,A,R[$T]),AND(T,B,R[$T]))`. The union rule (`:165-166`) splits that union before the bound of the type variable `T` is read, so `T <: union` is false (section 2.2) | `rows-686-687-689-690-normal-form.patch`: `normConjunct` expands a closed trait only against a conjunct that holds no type variable and no inference variable |
| 687 | 0 | The same normal form. In the coercion attempt (`typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:383`), the unifier applied to `$T <: union` gives an `Or`, and `Formula.slv` stops on it (`typechecker/Formula.scala:640`) | the same patch |
| 689 | 0 | The same: the plain attempt is refused as 686 is, and the coercion attempt then stops as 687 does | the same patch |
| 690 | 0 | The same normal form, at the meet of the two domains. `meet(T, K)` normalizes to `AND(T,OR(A,B))` instead of `T` (`overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:115`), and `subtypeUA` then finds no instance (`:117`) | the same patch |
| 685 | 4 (`:2464`, `:2837`, two each) | A library line, not the checker's scope. `array1` and `array2` call `vector[\T,s0\]()` (`:2454`) and `matrix[\T,s0,s1\]()` (`:2826`) with their own unbounded `T`, inside a `typecase` on `__thrower[\T\]`, which does not bound `T`. The checker's refusal is right. It names the callee's declared result because the call's type keeps the declaration's spans (`typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:137`, `:183`, `:158-165`) | `row-685-array-factories.patch`: the witness `typecase` per number type with `cast`, which is the library's own way (`additiveIdentity`, `:3229`) |
| 680 | crash row, 0 sites behind it | Nothing in `plane`'s body fails. The local function group's return-type thunks are primed with a TryChecker over the environment before the group is added (`typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:414`). So `plane`'s inferred return type is checked without its sibling `row` ('Variable `<row's unambiguous name>` not found', which the TryErrorLog keeps). `plane(k)` then comes back untyped in the loop's function expression (`typechecker/STypeChecker.scala:598-603`) | `row-680-local-function-group.patch`: prime the thunks with the checker that holds the group |

Fixed together: 54 → 49 (section 6). The sites cleared are the five that the brief names, 686's one and 685's four. No site appears that was not there before. Row 680's crash row is gone, and `Array3`'s body checks with no error, so nothing was hidden behind it.

A sibling outside the rows' tests (section 2.5): a call through a type parameter whose second bound names no type parameter (`T extends { K, Q }` with `Q excludes { C }`) still crashes after the normal-form fix. Two cases of the union rule repair it (`sibling-ground-bound.patch`). Its tracks are green, and it was not run in the distance stage.

## 2. Rows 686, 687, 689 and 690: one cause, in the analyzer's normal form

### 2.1 Reproduction

`repro/Bounds*.fss` are the four gated programs (`XXXInferCallerTwoBoundsClosedTrait` and its siblings) in the rows' shapes, plus the sibling. In each, `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `R[\T extends R[\T\]\]`, `A` and `B` extend `R`, and `C` does not. On the base (`old-fortress.sh <base> <caches> compile X.fss`):

    BoundsBoxArg.fss:11:48-50:  Could not check call to function h
        - [\T extends K R[\T\]\]Box[\T\]->T is not applicable to an argument of type Box[\T\].
    BoundsCallerParam:  ** bug! Applied a substitution to an And and got an Or
    BoundsNumeral:      ** bug! Applied a substitution to an And and got an Or
    BoundsReturnRule.fss:  For f, the return type of [\T extends K R[\T\]\]T->String ... should be a subtype of the return type of K->String

The two crashes go through the same frames (`fortress compile -debug stacktrace`): `Formula.slv(Formula.scala:640)` < `solveToBounds(:544)` < `STypesUtil.inferStaticParamsHelper(useful/STypesUtil.scala:1036)` < `Functionals.attempt$1(impls/Functionals.scala:383)` < `checkApplicableWithCoercion(:392)` < `typedApplicationOfChecked(:739)`. The ledger's `:593` and `:721` have drifted. The refusal is signalled at `Functionals.scala:755`.

### 2.2 The trace

- **The normal form.** `normConjunct` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:692-713`) has three branches.
  - First, if a conjunct definitely excludes a type that a closed conjunct lists, the closed conjunct becomes the union of its other listed types (`:693-698`).

## 5. The tracks

The run is `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks of `testFast`. It is the skill's command for a checker edit.

- **The three patches of sections 2.4, 3 and 4** (19 min 39 s under load 12 to 19):

      fast-compiler       Tests run: 1173, Failures: 4, Errors: 0
      fast-library        Tests run: 86, Failures: 0, Errors: 0
      fast-othercompiler  Tests run: 263, Failures: 0, Errors: 0

  The four failures are `XXXInferCallerTwoBoundsClosedTrait`, `XXXCoerceTwoBoundsClosedTrait`, `XXXCallerParamTwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `XXXReturnRuleTwoBoundsClosedTrait`, each 'Saw wrong failure. compile', because the programs now compile. The counts equal climb batch 14's gate (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-14/gate/summary.txt`).
- **The same with `sibling-ground-bound.patch` added** (9 min 24 s): the same three lines and the same four tests.
- **`ant testOnly`** for `TypeAnalyzerJUTest`, `TypeSchemaAnalyzerJUTest`, `FormulaJUTest` and `ConstraintJUTest`, in both states: 4, 4, 5 and 4 tests, no failure.
- **Not run:** the misc track's other classes, `testSystem` and the count stage. The library patch changes walk's library, which only `testSystem` and the demos run.

**The per-site comparison.** It compares the run's `errors.tsv` against `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, with the base's lines moved by the patch: +9 between the two factories, +16 after `array2`.

- Cleared:
  - the four `wellformed` sites of `Vector[\T,s0\]` and `Matrix[\T,s0,s1\]`, against `Number` and `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` (row 685);
  - `squaredNorm`'s 'not applicable to an argument of type Vector[\T,k\]' (row 686).
- Behind row 680: none.
- New sites: none. Three rows differ only in a second line number inside a span, which the comparison does not move.

**What the timings say.** The stage ran beside the tracks and other sessions' work, so its time is not comparable with batch 14's (1714 s at load 1.85). The patches' effect on the checker's speed is not measured. The count stage, with its 900-second limit (row 688), was not run. The normal-form patch makes the variable-bounded array family's bounds smaller, not larger, but that is a reading, not a measurement.

## 7. The rungs

The three fixes touch three declarations in three files: `TypeAnalyzer.normConjunct`, the `SLetFn` case of `impls/Decls.scala`, and `array1` and `array2` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`. None needs another: each was measured alone on its own reproducers, and the sites they clear are disjoint by site.

1. **The normal form (checker): rows 686, 687, 689, 690.** `rows-686-687-689-690-normal-form.patch`.
   - **Tests first:** promote the four `XXX` tests, with plain names, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`, as the skill's "Promoting an XXX test" says. Each fails on the base as a plain test (section 2.1) and passes with the patch.
   - **Distance:** -1 site. Row 688's count stage should be run once, since the normal form of every variable-bounded meet changes.
   - **Specification:** no sentence found that it makes false. The places searched were the Appendix I entries on bounds and closed traits, `basic/inference.tex` and `advanced/overloading.tex`.
   - **The sibling patch** belongs in this rung or in a later one, not in a parallel rung of the same batch. Alone, it also turns `XXXCoerceTwoBoundsClosedTrait` red, so two parallel rungs would both promote that test. Its test first is `repro/BoundsGround.fss` as a plain compiled test, which crashes on the base. With it, the rung should run the distance and count stages once more.
2. **The local function group (checker): row 680.** `row-680-local-function-group.patch`.
   - **Tests first:** `LocalFunctionSiblingInLoop` and `LocalFunctionSiblingCall` as `compiler_tests` with `typecheck` (from `repro/LocalSibling*.fss`; `link` is blocked by the LetFn wall). Both crash on the base. A third test from `repro/LocalRecursiveUntyped.fss`, with `compile_err_contains=reference cycle`, can carry the recursive case.
   - **Distance:** the crash row goes, 0 sites.
   - **Specification:** none made false. The rationale of Appendix I's "revival-paramtype" entry (`changes.tex:3317-3333`) lists the crash messages of rows 620 to 622 as history, and it stays true.
3. **The array factories (library): row 685.** `row-685-array-factories.patch`.
   - **Tests first:** a walk test in `ProjectFortress/tests/` from `repro/ArrayFactoryWalk.fss`, which is a guard that passes before and after. Beside it, the assertions of `repro/ArrayFactoryAbstract.fss` that an abstract number type gives a plain array, which fail on the base.
   - **Distance:** -4 sites.
   - **Specification:** `Specification/appendices/future.tex:263-264` becomes false (section 8).

## 10. Decisions

- **The normal-form fix keeps the team's expansion for ground meets.** The alternatives were:
  - removing the expansion altogether, which also clears the sibling and was not run through the tracks;
  - adding the union-rule cases alone, which clear 687 and the sibling only;
  - a guard in `slv`, which clears 687 only and turns 689 into a refusal.

  The kept fix is the smallest change that clears the four rows, and it holds the POPL 2019 condition that no union built by the checker holds a type parameter (section 2.4). No decision of the curator covers the analyzer's normal form.
- **Row 685's fix follows the library's witness `typecase` with `cast`,** not a checker rule that would let a `typecase` on `__thrower[\T\]` bound `T`. That would be a language change, which is the curator's. The patch's one change in walk's results, abstract number types, is listed in section 3 and section 8.
- **Row 680's fix is the checker's.** `plane`'s line is valid Fortress by `basic/functions.tex`. The library workaround, writing `: ()`, is noted and not used.
- **The distance stage is `distance/run.sh`.** The brief's parenthesis names `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`, which is the walk test-count runner. The stage it describes, the distance (26 to 29 minutes), is `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`, and that is what ran.
- **The note itself.** It could not be written as a file by the probe agent: the session's tool guard refused it. The probe committed the patches, the reproducers and the script (`32269d57d`), and handed this text over.

## 11. For the curator

**Row 685's record.** The question: is row 685 retired, its claim falsified (the checker's refusal is right), and replaced by proposed rows 2 and 3?

- Sources: this note, section 3; `Specification/appendices/future.tex:257-264` (the revival's box, 2026); the team's TODO at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2451`.
- Solutions:
  - (a) Retire 685 and add rows 2 and 3.
  - (b) Rewrite 685's claim to row 2's and add row 3.
- Current behaviour: the record stays as it is, either way, until rung 3 lands.

**The sibling patch's place.** The question: does `sibling-ground-bound.patch` go into rung 1, wait for a later rung, or give way to removing the expansion?

- Sources: section 2.5. `Papers/Types/fig-subtype.tick` is the team's 2011 paper; the POPL 2019 paper is one of the type group's late positions.
- Each changes:
  - In rung 1: no library site needs it, and it changes row 518's mechanism.
  - A later rung: the sibling row stays open.
  - Removing the expansion: the team's precision for ground meets is lost, unmeasured on the tracks.
- The current behaviour stays with "a later rung".

## 12. For FACTS

- **F-94 is to be rewritten.**
  - **The fact:** the compiled checker's failures at a type parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound excluding one of its listed types (rows 686, 687, 689, 690) have one cause. `TypeAnalyzer.normConjunct` expands the closed trait over a conjunct that holds a variable, and the first-match union rule then loses the variable's instance. One change there clears all four, and a solver guard does not.
  - **What it means:** one checker rung, not an inference rung, and a second change for the ground sibling.
  - **The number:** 1 distance site (686).
  - **The tests:** the four `XXX` tests, which turn red with the fix.
  - **Detail:** this note, sections 2.2 to 2.5.
- **A new fact.**
  - **The fact:** the compiled checker infers a local function's return type without its group in scope (`impls/Decls.scala:414`). So a local function with no written return type that calls a sibling crashes the checker, from a loop body or directly, and `Array3`'s `asString` is the library's case.
  - **What it means:** row 680 is a one-line checker rung, and nothing waits behind it.
  - **The number:** 0 sites.
  - **The test:** `repro/LocalSiblingInLoop.fss` with `fortress typecheck`, which crashes on the base.
  - **Detail:** section 4.
- **Row 685 is a library line.**
  - **The fact:** `array1` and `array2` instantiate the bounded factories at their unbounded `T`.
  - **The number:** 4 distance sites.
  - **The check:** the distance stage's two `wellformed` pairs.
  - **Detail:** section 3.

## 13. Commands worked out

- **The quick loop on a Scala file.** Compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d DIR X.scala`, then run `com.sun.fortress.Shell compile` with `DIR` first on the class path. This is `references/compiler.md`'s loop.
  - Against the base build's classes and caches, `CP` must come from the base's `bin/fortress_classpath` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base.
  - Several fixes were compared without rebuilding, behind `-D` switches in a probe copy of `TypeAnalyzer.scala`.
- **`mini-distance.sh` (beside this note).** It runs the distance stage's checker, in the "any" setting with every stage, over small components that import the interpreter library, without checking the apis with every stage. That takes about 3 minutes instead of about 30, so a library body copied into its own component can be bisected.
- **Hidden checker errors.** To see an error that a TryChecker's log swallows, print `tryChecker.getError` where `Thunker.makeThunk` gets `None`, and `nameHasBinding` of the names in scope at `Misc.scala:162`.

(** The two-argument version of %member% returns the default value %v%
        if the key is absent from the map. **)
    member(x:ZZ64, v:Val): Val =
        if x=key then val else v end
    (** %minimum% and %maximum% refer to the key. **)
    minimum():Just[\(ZZ64,Val)\] = Just[\(ZZ64,Val)\](key,val)
    deleteMinimum():IntMap[\Val\] = EmptyIM[\Val\]
    extractMinimum():Just[\(ZZ64,Val, IntMap[\Val\])\] =
        Just[\(ZZ64,Val, IntMap[\Val\])\](key,val, EmptyIM[\Val\])
    maximum(): Just[\(ZZ64,Val)\] = minimum()
    deleteMaximum():IntMap[\Val\] = EmptyIM[\Val\]
    extractMaximum():Just[\(ZZ64,Val, IntMap[\Val\])\] = extractMinimum()

    (** If no mapping presently exists, maps %k% to %v%. **)
    add(k:ZZ64, v:Val):NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] =
        if k=key then self
        else addU(k,v) end
    add(s:SingletonIM[\Val\]):NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] =
        if s.key=key then self else addU(s) end
    (** As %add%, but throws %KeyOverlap% if %k% is already mapped. **)
    addNew(s:SingletonIM[\Val\]): NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] =
    if s.key=key then throw KeyOverlap(key,val,s.val)
        else addU(s) end
    (** Internal: update with given singleton node **)
    update(n:SingletonIM[\Val\]): NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] =
        if n.key = key then n
        else addU(n) end
    addU(k:ZZ64, v:Val): NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] = addU(SingletonIM[\Val\](k,v))
    addU(s:SingletonIM[\Val\]): NonEmptyIntMap[\Val\] =
        if s.key < key then s.ordJoin(self)
        else self.ordJoin(s)
        end
    (** Eliminate any mapping for key %k%. **)
    delete(k:ZZ64):IntMap[\Val\] = if k=key then EmptyIM[\Val\] else self end
    (** Process mapping for key %k% with function %f%:
        \begin{itemize}
        \item If no mapping exists, %f% is passed %Nothing[\Val\]%
        \item If %k% maps to value %v%, %f% is passed %Just[\Val\](v)%
        \end{itemize}
        If %f% returns %Nothing%, any mapping for %k% is deleted; otherwise,
        %k% is mapped to the value contained in the result.
     **)
    updateWith(f:Maybe[\Val\]->Maybe[\Val\], k:ZZ64): IntMap[\Val\] =
        if k=key then
            if v <- f(Just[\Val\](val)) then
                SingletonIM[\Val\](k,v)
            else
                EmptyIM[\Val\]
            end
        elif v <- f(Nothing[\Val\]) then
            self.add(k,v)
        else
            self
        end
    (** %UNION% favors the leftmost value when a key occurs in both maps. **)

(* IntMap's UPLUS of a many-entry map and a one-entry map on a shared key, whose value under walk throws KeyOverlap only with the one-entry map on the left. *)
component IntMapUplusSingleton
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

overlap(f: () -> IntMap[\ZZ32\]): String = do
    msg: String := "no exception"
    try
        ignore(f())
    catch e
        UncheckedException => msg := e.asString
    end
    msg
  end

run(): () = do
    three = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#3}
    one = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 9}
    five = {[\ZZ32\] widen(5) |-> 5}
    all4 = {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(1) |-> 1, widen(2) |-> 2, widen(5) |-> 5}
    assert(three UPLUS five, all4, "a many-entry map UPLUS a one-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(five UPLUS three, all4, "a one-entry map UPLUS a many-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(overlap(fn () => one UPLUS three), "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 1 |-> 1 and |-> 9", "a one-entry map UPLUS a many-entry map holding its key throws KeyOverlap")

component IntMapSymdiffSingleton
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

run(): () = do
    three = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#3}
    five = {[\ZZ32\] widen(5) |-> 5}
    one = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 1}
    assert(five SYMDIFF three, {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(1) |-> 1, widen(2) |-> 2, widen(5) |-> 5}, "a one-entry map SYMDIFF a many-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(one SYMDIFF three, {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(2) |-> 2}, "a one-entry map SYMDIFF a many-entry map holding its key drops that key")
    assert(three SYMDIFF five, {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(1) |-> 1, widen(2) |-> 2, widen(5) |-> 5}, "a many-entry map SYMDIFF a one-entry map on another key holds all four entries")
    assert(three SYMDIFF one, {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(2) |-> 2}, "a many-entry map SYMDIFF a one-entry map holding its key drops that key")

    assert(|evens SYMDIFF four|, 4, "a many-entry map of five SYMDIFF a one-entry map holding its key has four entries")
    assert(evens SYMDIFF seven, seven SYMDIFF evens, "a many-entry map SYMDIFF a one-entry map on another key is the reverse order's map")
    assert(|evens SYMDIFF seven|, 6, "a many-entry map of five SYMDIFF a one-entry map on another key has six entries")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

component IntMapTest
export Executable
import IntMap.{...}
import List.{...}
import Shuffle.{...}

assEq(a:IntMap[\ZZ32\], b:IntMap[\ZZ32\], msg:Any...): () =
    if a.check()=/=b.check() then
        println(toDots(a,b))
        fail((BIG || msg) // a // "=/=" // b)
    end

run(): () = do
    me = {[\ZZ32\] }
    mz = {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 1}
    m0 = {[\ZZ32\] widen(x) |-> (x+5) | x <- (-7):57:3}
    a = toArray((-7):57:3)
    shuffle(a)
    m1 = {[\ZZ32\] widen(i) |-> (i+5) | i <- a }
    b = toArray((-3):17)
    shuffle(b)
    m2 = {[\ZZ32\] widen(i) |-> i | i <- b }
    maps = <| me, mz, m0, m1, m2 |>
    checkedMaps = maps.map[\IntMap[\ZZ32\]\](fn (m:IntMap[\ZZ32\]):IntMap[\ZZ32\] => m.check)
    (* Test member *)
    for i <- (-8):58 do
        assert(m0.member(i).holds, ((i+7) MOD 3) = 0)
    end
    (* Test equality *)
    assEq(me,me)
    assEq(mz,mz)
    assEq(m0,m0)
    assEq(m0,m1)
    assEq(m2,m2)
    assert(m1=m2, false, m1, "=", m2)
    (* Test add *)
    assEq(me.add(0,1),mz)
    assEq(mz.add(0,17),mz)
    assEq(m0.add(5,15), m0)
    assert(m0.add(6,17).member(6).get, 17)
    (* Test update *)
    assEq(me.update(0,1),mz)
    assert(mz.update(0,17).member(0).get, 17)
    assert(m0.update(5,15).member(5).get, 15)
    assert(m0.update(6,17).member(6).get, 17)
    (* Test DIFFERENCE *)
    diffSpec(x,y) = {[\ZZ32\] i |-> v | (i,v) <- x, NOT (y.member(i).holds) }
    assEq(me DIFFERENCE m0, me, "Difference E")
    assEq(mz DIFFERENCE mz, me, "Difference Z")
    assEq(m0 DIFFERENCE mz, m0, "Difference EE")
    assEq(m2.delete(0), m2 DIFFERENCE mz, "Difference Delete")
    assEq(diffSpec(m2,m1), m2 DIFFERENCE m1, "Difference 1 of\n", m2, "\nand\n", m1)
    assEq(diffSpec(m1,m2), m1 DIFFERENCE m2, "Difference 2")
    (* Test UNION *)
    unionSpec(x,y) = {[\ZZ32\] i |-> v | m <- <|x,y DIFFERENCE x|>, (i,v) <- m }
    assEq(me UNION me, me, "Union E")
    assEq(mz UNION mz, mz, "Union Z")
    assEq(me UNION mz, mz, "Union Z'")
    assEq(mz UNION me, mz, "Union Z\"")
    assEq(m2 UNION mz, m2, "Union m2")
    assEq(unionSpec(m0,m2), m0 UNION m2, "Union 1")
    (* Test INTERSECTION *)
    interSpec(x,y) = {[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] i |-> (v1,v2) | (i,v1) <- x, v2 <- y.member(i) }
    fst(m:IntMap[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]) = m.map[\ZZ32\](fn (_:ZZ64,v:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):ZZ32 => do (x,y) = v; x end)
    inter(x,y) = x.intersection[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]((fn (_:ZZ64,z:ZZ32,_:ZZ32): ZZ32 => z), y)
    assEq(inter(me, me), me)
    assEq(inter(mz, me), me)
    assEq(inter(mz, mz), mz)
    assEq(inter(m0, m0), m0)
    assEq(inter(m0, mz), me)
    assEq(inter(mz, m2), mz)
    assEq(inter(m0,m2), fst(m0 INTERSECTION m2))
    assEq(inter(m2,m0), fst(m2 INTERSECTION m0))
    (* Test SYMDIFF *)
    symdiffSpec(x,y) = (x UNION y) DIFFERENCE (x INTERSECTION y)
    assEq(symdiffSpec(m0,m2), m0 SYMDIFF m2, "Symdiff 1")
    assEq(me SYMDIFF me, me)
    assEq(mz SYMDIFF mz, me)
    assEq(me SYMDIFF mz, mz)
    assEq(mz SYMDIFF me, mz)
    assEq(me SYMDIFF m2, m2)
    (* Test delete *)
    assEq(mz.delete(0),me)
    assEq(mz.delete(1),mz)
    assEq(m0.delete(0),m0)
    assert(m2.delete(0), m2 DIFFERENCE mz)
    println("OK")
  end

end
(* IntMap's combine calls its function on each key both maps hold, and its two map functions on the parts that only one map holds. *)
component IntMapCombine
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

addValues(k: ZZ64, a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): Maybe[\ZZ32\] = Just[\ZZ32\](a + b)
dropKey(k: ZZ64, a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): Maybe[\ZZ32\] = Nothing[\ZZ32\]
keepAll(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = m
dropAll(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = {[\ZZ32\] }
tenTimes(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = m.map[\ZZ32\](fn (k: ZZ64, v: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 10 v)

run(): () = do
    noEntry = {[\ZZ32\] }
    oneEntry = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10}
    sameKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 5}
    otherKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(2) |-> 5}
    farKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(-100) |-> 7}
    eight = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#8}
    upper = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> 100 | k <- 4#8}

    assert(noEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, noEntry).isEmpty, true, "two empty maps combine to the empty map")
    assert(noEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), oneEntry, "the empty map combined with a map gives that map's part through the second map function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, noEntry).check(), oneEntry, "a map combined with the empty map gives its part through the first map function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, sameKey).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 15}, "two one-entry maps on one key combine their values by the function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](dropKey, keepAll, keepAll, sameKey).isEmpty, true, "a key whose function answers Nothing is left out")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, otherKey).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10, widen(2) |-> 5}, "two one-entry maps on different keys combine to both entries")
    assert(otherKey.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10, widen(2) |-> 5}, "the order of the maps does not change the entries of two maps on different keys")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, dropAll, dropAll, otherKey).isEmpty, true, "two one-entry maps on different keys share no key")

    both = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 100 end) | k <- 0#12}
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, upper).check(), both, "two many-entry maps combine the keys both hold and keep the others")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, dropAll, dropAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k + 100 | k <- 4#4}, "two many-entry maps with both map functions dropping keep only the keys both hold")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](dropKey, keepAll, keepAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k else 100 end) | k <- 0#12, k < 4 OR k >= 8}, "two many-entry maps with the function answering Nothing keep the keys only one holds")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, tenTimes, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 1000 end) | k <- 0#12}, "the second map function maps the keys only the second map holds")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, tenTimes, keepAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then 10 k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 100 end) | k <- 0#12}, "the first map function maps the keys only the first map holds")

    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k = 1 then 11 else k end) | k <- 0#8}, "a many-entry map combined with a one-entry map on a key it holds")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, eight).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k = 1 then 11 else k end) | k <- 0#8}, "a one-entry map combined with a many-entry map on a key it holds")
    assert(|eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, farKey).check()|, 9, "a many-entry map combined with a one-entry map on a key below all of its keys")
    assert(farKey.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, eight).check().member(widen(-100)).get, 7, "a one-entry map on a key below all of a many-entry map's keys keeps its entry")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

## 2. Your questions, in the order they block the batch

**No question blocks the batch, and none is open.** The questions the two probes raised, and where walk's collector goes, are settled by the record's principles, as calls of the coordinator's under your rule for forks (`coordinator/BOOT.md`, "How forks reach him"); they are listed for your review below with their bases.

### The coordinator's calls this batch builds, listed for your review

Each is settled by the record's principles and is reversible; none reverses a decision of yours. Call 1 reads past the letter of one, P-48's last clause, as the walk probe asked to confirm (its section 1).

1. **Walk fixes an unwritten clause form's parameter by its elements: way 6 + 7** (the walk probe's question 1). The specification's desugaring fixes that parameter by the expression's type `N` (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`, figure `generatedExpressions`). The record already reads walk's run-time element types as walk's counterpart of `N` (F-143; `Specification/basic/inference.tex:367-369`). entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

content.content:
### Climb batch 14, listed for his review

The items climb batch 14's rungs, skeptics and gather left for him (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-14/RECORD.md`). None blocks a batch or the switch-over unless its entry under "Pavol's answers" says so; each is reversible, and the default is what landed.

- L.worker.2 and L.skeptic.2 of climb batch 14's rung L: row 703 records walk's refusal of the typed `body(i: I)` as a new row, while review-queue item 17 says its case 'has no open row and this entry is its record' (`explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md:132`) and lists such a row among its other ways. Keep the row, which records a consequence, the count's error, or fold its text into item 17? Default: the row as filed. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-library-followups/REPORT.md:188` (decision 6). The coordinator's call (2026-10-14, by his rule of 00:12 UTC): review-queue item 17 is settled by P-48, a parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, never `Bottom`; walk's D2 departure is engineering, probed before batch 15 (`perf-probes/walk-plain-bound/REPORT.md`), and typing `body(i)` follows it.
- L.skeptic.3 of climb batch 14's rung L: should a later rung repair row 704? `IntMap`'s `NodeIM` `UPLUS` with a one-entry map is `self.add(other)` (`Library/IntMap.fss:520`), which keeps the many-entry map's value on a shared key, while the reverse order throws `KeyOverlap` (`:340`) and the comment promises the throw (`:517-518`). The library's own way would be `self.addNew(other)` (`:488-490`), turning today's quiet value into `KeyOverlap`. The specification is silent on `IntMap`. Default: today's value, pinned by `ProjectFortress/tests/IntMapUplusSingleton.fss`. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-library-followups/SKEPTIC.md:78`. The coordinator's call (2026-10-14, by his rule of 00:12 UTC): yes, by the library's own `addNew`, which throws on a shared key as the comment promises; a later library rung, today's value pinned until then.
- A.worker.1 and A.skeptic.1 of climb batch 14's rung A: P-51's retry reaches a reduction's big operator, which the desugaring writes as a call that is an argument of `__bigOperator` (half of row 425): with an expected type, a plain-bounded big operator now takes it where the instance at its bound does not fit, so `s: ZZ32 = BIG LAST[j <- lo#n] (3 j)` with the bound `Number`, refused before, runs; an F-bounded one is still refused. The probe's measurement did not cover this reach; P-51's wording does. Does he accept it? Default: as built. The three boxes that said the checker takes the bound are corrected (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:345-352`, `Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:38-44`, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1056-1060`). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/InferBigOperatorExpectedType.fss:30`; `compile-ladder/rung-argument-context/REPORT.md:153` (section 7).
- A.worker.2 and A.skeptic.2 of climb batch 14's rung A: the argument retry's forks 2, 4 and 5, on the review list (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-14.md:91-94`), as built. Fork 2: a generic enclosing declaration is instantiated from the arguments not retried and the call's expected type. Fork 4: a tie among retried declarations is refused with today's message, 'not applicable to an argument of type BoxT[\Object\]', the argument's type without the expected type, not as an ambiguity (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:892-895`; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXInferCallArgumentControls.fss:17`). Fork 5: an argument that writes its static arguments is retried, to the same type. The patch left such an argument out of the enclosing call's instantiation, against fork 5's 'to no effect'; the skeptic followed P-51's definition of the retried argument, so such an argument now instantiates the enclosing declaration (`Functionals.scala:867`, `:910-924`; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/InferCallArgumentWrittenStaticArgs.fss:14-15`). Is that the reading he wants, with fork 4's message? Default: as built. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-argument-context/SKEPTIC.md:54` (finding 1).
- A.worker.3 and A.skeptic.4 of climb batch 14's rung A: walk gives a call written as another call's argument no expected type (row 705). `takesBox64(mk())` fails at run time, 'got arg BoxT[\Any\]'; where another declaration accepts the argument at its bound, walk runs it: `f(Any)` where the compiled path runs `f(BoxT[ZZ64])`, and the binary `OPLUS` where it runs the multifix one. Whether and where walk should fix an argument's static arguments from the enclosing declaration's parameter type (at dispatch, a site other than row 510's typed binding) is his. Default: the expected failure. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXInferCallArgumentWalk.fss:15`; row 705. The coordinator's call (2026-10-14, by his rule of 00:12 UTC): as landed; walk takes the checker's static types at the switch-over (P-59), which closes it.
- A.skeptic.3 of climb batch 14's rung A: should the argument context reach a call without static arguments? A call of a non-generic overloaded function whose own argument needs the context stays refused: `takesBox64(p(mk()))`, with `p` declared on `BoxT[\ZZ64\]` and on `BoxT[\ZZ32\]`, is refused, while `bound(): BoxT[\ZZ64\] = p(mk())` compiles. P-51 retries only a call with inferred static arguments, and the chapter now says so (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:150`). Default: as P-51 says. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-argument-context/SKEPTIC.md:154` (section 3, `SkPlainInner`).
- P.worker.1 and P.skeptic.1 of climb batch 14's rung P, beside climb batch 11's gather.1 and climb batch 12's gather.2 above (the gap ledger's tool has no route for some writes): `ledger.py` only appends notes and has no command that sets a row's reproducer cell (`explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py:778-792`). Rows 373, 444, 697, 698 and 699 read `none` although tests now gate them, and rows 444 and 697 have no room left even for a note (their notes cells hold 683 and 681 of 700 characters). Their tests: row 444, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXDottedMethodMeetBothBodiesWalk.fss`; row 697, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXReturnRuleObjectParamWalk.fss`; row 373, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXGenericBoundsNoMeetWalk.fss`. How should these tests be named on their rows? Default: the notes the rung wrote on rows 373, 698 and 699, and none on 444 and 697. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md:248` (section 12).

trait AnyAppend extends AnyCovColl
    getter a(): Any
    getter b(): Any
end

private object Append[\T,A extends T, B extends T\](a:NonEmpty[\A\], b:NonEmpty[\B\])
        extends { AnyAppend, NonEmpty[\T\] }
    sz = |a| + |b|
    opr |self|: ZZ32 = sz
    unapp[\R\](k:(NonEmpty[\A\], NonEmpty[\B\])->R): R = k(a,b)
    cata[\R\](e:R, s:T->R, app:(ZZ32,R,R)->R): R = app(sz,a.cata[\R\](e,s,app),b.cata[\R\](e,s,app))
    dirtyIAF[\R\](arr:ImmutableArray[\R,ZZ32\], i:ZZ32): () = do
        a.dirtyIAF[\R\](arr,i)
      also do
        b.dirtyIAF[\R\](arr,i + |a|)
      end
end

object CVReduction[\T\] extends MonoidReduction[\AnyCovColl\]
    getter asString():String = "CV Reduction"
    empty(): AnyCovColl = Empty[\T\]
    join(a:AnyCovColl, b:AnyCovColl): AnyCovColl = a APPCOV b
end

CVSingleton(a:Any): AnyCovColl = Singleton(a)

covariantCompr[\T,R\](unwrap:AnyCovColl->R):Comprehension[\T,R,AnyCovColl,AnyCovColl\] =

end

  a1 = array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => i i + 1)
  assert(a1[0] " " a1[1] " " a1[2] " " a1[3], "1 2 5 10", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", 1-D")
  f1 = tabulatedArray1[\RR64,3\](fn (i:ZZ32):RR64 => 2.0 i)

  s1 = array1[\ZZ32,3\]().shift(5).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)
  assert(s1[5] " " s1[6] " " s1[7], "50 60 70", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", at each index of a shifted array")
  m1 = immutableArray[\ZZ32\](3).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 7 - i)

  a2 = array[\ZZ32\](2,3).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i + j)
  assert(a2[0,0] " " a2[0,2] " " a2[1,0] " " a2[1,2], "0 2 10 12", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", 2-D")

Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex
\seclabel{typecase}

\note{This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal.}

\note{Do we want to support \EXP{\KWD{typecase} \mathord{\KWD{self}} \KWD{of} \ldots}?

How about \EXP{\KWD{typecase} (x, \KWD{self}, y) \KWD{of} \ldots}?

[07/23/2007] \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}} is not allowed in a shorthand form of
\KWD{typecase} expresiosn.
% foo(x) = 8
% bar(x) = 3
% trait Parent
%    foo(x) = 10
%    baz(x) =
%      typecase self of
%        Child => bar(x)
%        Parent => 23
%      end
% end
% trait Child extends Parent
%    bar(x) = foo(x)
% end
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \VAR{foo}(x) = 8\)\\
\( \VAR{bar}(x) = 3\)\\
\( \KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Parent}\)\\
{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{foo}(x) = 10\)\\
\(    \VAR{baz}(x) =\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(      \KWD{typecase} \mathord{\KWD{self}} \KWD{of}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(        \TYP{Child} \Rightarrow \VAR{bar}(x)\)\\
\(        \TYP{Parent} \Rightarrow 23\)\-\\\poptabs
\(      \KWD{end}\)\-\-\\\poptabs\poptabs
\( \KWD{end}\)\\
\( \KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Child} \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Parent}\)\\
{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{bar}(x) = \VAR{foo}(x)\)\-\\\poptabs
\( \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}
}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{DelimitedExpr}
&::=& \KWD{typecase} \emph{TypecaseBindings} \KWD{of}
\emph{TypecaseClauses} \option{\emph{CaseElse}} \KWD{end}\\

\emph{TypecaseBindings} &::=& \emph{TypecaseVars}
\options{\EXP{=} \emph{Expr}}\\

\emph{TypecaseVars} &::=& \emph{BindId} \\
&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^+$ \texttt{)} \\

\emph{TypecaseClauses} &::=& \emph{TypecaseClause}$^+$\\

\emph{TypecaseClause} &::=&
\emph{TypecaseTypes} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems} \\

\emph{TypecaseTypes}
&::=& \texttt{(} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{Type} \\

\emph{CaseElse} &::=& \KWD{else} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems}\\

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's checker (explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh, setting
# "any") over small components that import the interpreter library, in seconds to a few
# minutes instead of the stage's half hour: the apis are not checked with every stage
# (probe.componentOnly), so only the named components' bodies are. It shows a crash or an
# error of a library body copied into a component of its own, as Array3AsStringProbe.fss
# shows row 680. Run from the tree's root, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/perf-probes/checker-bound-defects/mini-distance.sh <scratch-dir> <file.fss>...
#
# The first call builds the stage's shadow classes into <scratch-dir> (run.sh's step 1);
# later calls reuse them, so remove <scratch-dir> after an edit of the checker. Each
# component's result is a line per declaration: @@TC DECL-OK, DECL-ERR or DECL-CRASH.
set -u
S=${1:?usage: mini-distance.sh <scratch-dir> <file.fss>...}; shift
case "$S" in /*) ;; *) S="$PWD/$S" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance"
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's#:[^:]*/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache##')
if [ ! -f "$S/classes/DistanceMulti.class" ] ; then
    rm -rf "$S/shadow-src" "$S/shadow-classes" "$S/classes"
    mkdir -p "$S/shadow-src" "$S/shadow-classes" "$S/classes"
    ( cd "$FH" && python3 "$D/shadow-patch.py" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress "$S/shadow-src" \
               && python3 "$D/add-patch.py" "$S/shadow-src" ) > "$S/shadows.txt" 2>&1 || { echo "shadow edits stale: $S/shadows.txt" ; exit 1 ; }
    javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d "$S/shadow-classes" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/TypeCheckPhase.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/DesugarPhase.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Desugarer.java" \
        "$S/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeComparator.java" >> "$S/shadows.txt" 2>&1 \
      && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$S/classes" "$D/DistanceMulti.java" >> "$S/shadows.txt" 2>&1 \
      || { echo "shadow classes did not compile: $S/shadows.txt" ; exit 1 ; }
fi
rm -rf "$S/caches" "$S/tmp" ; mkdir -p "$S/caches" "$S/tmp"
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 30 3600 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow \
      -Djava.io.tmpdir="$S/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$S/caches" \
      -Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dprobe.componentOnly=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false \
      -cp "$S/shadow-classes:$S/classes:$CP" DistanceMulti -order check -setting any "$@" )

## 1. 2026-09-15: the open question

### Sources

The 2026-09-15 exchange is not in the coordinating session's own transcript. That session (`fe616d40-…`) has records for 09-08, 09-09, 09-14, then 09-18 onward. The 09-15 session is the earlier archived one, `bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6`, on the `transcripts` branch (`origin/transcripts`, `projects/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6.jsonl.parts/001.jsonl`). It is not on `transcripts-blinded`. Line numbers below are lines of that part file. The 2026-09-19 and later exchanges are in `fe616d40-…until-2026-10-08T15-41.jsonl.parts/000.jsonl`.

### What the extensions were

The model program's vocabulary was a component of its own, `FlatArrays` (C4: `explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi` and `.fss`; the APL focused base had a smaller copy, `FlatArrays2`, in `apl/mg/`). The run's brief had told the worker that "everything you need beyond [the shipped library] is user-level code in your own component" (`explorations/reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §2). The review of 2026-09-19 inventories it (`reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §1): 38 declarations, of which 5 are aliases of library calls, 26 are new operations over the library's own `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix` and `Array3`, and 9 are new structures (eight view objects and `Diag`). The 35 new things (26 operations and 9 structures), by family:

| family | declarations (names in `FlatArrays.fsi`) |
|---|---|
| scalar extension of `RR64` arrays | `+` and `-` with a scalar in both orders, `MAX` with a scalar |
| elementwise algebra | `×`, `/` (array by array and by scalar), `>`, `SQRT`, `exp`, `log` |
| rank-3 algebra | plane-wise `+` of a matrix to every plane of an `Array3`; batched product of two `Array3` |
| the diagonal | `Diag`, `diag`, `Diag` times a matrix |
| views (the 9 structures) | `view`, `row`, `row3`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane`, the transposes |
| the row lift | `rows`, four overloads |
| keys | `gather`, `onehot`, `pick`, `flat` |

The library had almost nothing of this: scalar extension only for one-dimensional integer arrays, array first, and only `+ - MIN MAX` (`opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)`, `git show 02d09a39f^:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, lines 2535-2538); scalar `DOT` and juxtaposition in both orders on `Vector` and `Matrix`; no elementwise `×` or `/` (only `Vector`'s `pmul`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1609`, `:1647`); no rank-3 algebra, no `gather`, no `rows` (§2 of the same review).

### How the question came up

On 2026-09-15 he reviewed `FlatArrays.fsi` (40 declarations at the time). At 08:25:05 he wrote (line 10420):

> It looks like our extensions are working with specific type combinations here. And it seems like we are not expressing a generic form that could collapse the number of needed definitions. Do we have a good reason? Like this all looks like the code after type inference and specialization. For our specific use case. So my general feeling is just that if we are trying to express some extension of a functionality to standard fortress types, we should not be limiting the definitions and implementations to our specific cases. And I think what I see here is mostly operator operator overloading, etc. And I am not seeing this this fortress specific Uh, algebraic type definitions that give us traits for free.

At 10:42:06 (line 10966), after the coordinator had named Ring and Field without explaining them (he says so below; the explanation came at 10:45) and had reported that the shipped `RR64` does not satisfy the specification's `AdditiveGroup`:

> I think that fleshing out the standard library is one very important task to close it. So, the bug that you found in the algebraic constraints, what was it? That the uh, shipped RR64 does not even satisfy the specs additive group. Like, we should. First, finish that one and then apply those principles and, and go to the higher dimension. [...] Extending the, the library flavor that was given with the existing things like the additive glue, group, multiplicative ring, etc. Uh, like I'd like to see that shape of the library extended so that the expression expressing the machine learning concepts with the matrices and tensors have the mathematical rigor that this flavor of library construction promises.

### The two choices, as the coordinator put them

At 10:45:07 (line 11020):

> **"Fleshing out the standard library."** Recorded as your position. One question only you can answer, and I have not assumed the answer: the standing rule is that `Library/` is never modified, and this direction reads as modifying it. The alternative is building the algebraic layer in our own tree, over the shipped traits, which is what every run so far has done. Worklist item 4 is literally "unseal the linear-algebra layer", five rows. Say which.

At 11:02:11 (line 11056), among three items waiting on him:

> 2. Whether "fleshing out the standard library" means editing the sealed `Library/`, which the standing rule forbids, or building the algebraic layer in our own tree over the shipped traits.

So the choices were:

- **Edit the sealed `Library/`.** The standing rule came from 2026-08-30 11:11:46, when the coordinator offered to unseal `Number` by one token and he answered "We are not unsealing anything!!! You’re again claiming something is impossible with your self imposed constraints." (line 1414). The exploration treated the original tree as a historical artifact (his words of 09-16, below).
- **Build it in "our own tree".** That meant what every run had done: the project's own components next to the shipped library (C4's `FlatArrays`, the focused base's `FlatArrays2`), over the library's traits, with `Library/` untouched. The coordinator's default, recorded at 10:44 (`POSITIONS-history.md:19`), was this one "until he says otherwise".

At 2026-09-15 21:14:56 he answered the three items (line 11066):

> 1. ?!?
> 2. Later
> 3. Yes

On 2026-09-16 22:43:26 he already spoke of the change as coming (line 12007): "as we go into unsealing the library and we start changing what the fortress is. Uh, until now we've approached it as, as a historical artifact". On 2026-09-17 the tree was tagged `sealed-tree` (`75cca6683`) and later commits were allowed to edit the original sources, test first (`POSITIONS-history.md:25`). Whether the library was meant was still the open item until 09-19.

content.content:
A $k$-dimensional array \VAR{A} is indexed by placing a sequence of
$k$ indices enclosed in brackets, and separated by commas, after an expression
evaluating to \VAR{A}.
Thus, the index is rendered as a subscript.
By default, arrays are indexed from 0.  The
horizontal dimension of an array is the last dimension mentioned in the
array index.  For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Array.a.tex}
then \EXP{A_{1,0}} evaluates to \EXP{4}.

pasted along dimension 0. Each row is pasted along dimension 1 and the
resulting matrix is ``flattened''.  This works because matrices never
contain other matrices as elements.

a row (or column) must have the same number of columns (or rows),

\subsection{The implicit bound of a type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-bound}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{type-param}; \secref{principles-overloading}.
\item[Change] A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause has the
implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' in place of
``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'', with a box.
The restriction of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} that a functional whose
single parameter's type is a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} cannot be
overloaded is stated for a bound written \TYP{Any}, and a sentence says that a
type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause does not fall under it,
with \library's value factory of one-dimensional arrays as its example, and a
box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival took
\TYP{Any} as the implicit bound on 27~September 2026 and decided it on
29~September 2026.
\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples, functions and \TYP{()} among them; the
team's later Types chapter makes \TYP{Object} a supertype of every trait type,
arrow type and function type that excludes \TYP{()} and every tuple type
(Luchangco, 2012,
\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
232--236, in the revival's repository).
\Library\ instantiate type parameters declared without a bound at tuple types,
an array indexed by pairs among them, which the bound \TYP{Object} would refuse;
the interpreter, and the compiled type checker when it checks \library, read
such a parameter as bounded by \TYP{Any}.
The type group's paper of 2019 gives the same default: ``By default, each type
parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom'' (Park, Hong, Steele
and Ryu, POPL 2019, Section~3.2).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any}, the restriction on a naked type parameter of
bound \TYP{Any} would forbid overloading every functional whose single
parameter's type is a type parameter declared without a bound, \library's
factory \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()} among them;
the compiled type checker applies the restriction only to a bound written
\TYP{Any}, and draws no such refusal on \library.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A type parameter declared without a bound may be instantiated
with a tuple type or with \TYP{()}.
The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a
divergence that lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the
interpreter's library.
The rationale of \secref{revival-tabulate}, written before this change, speaks
of the implicit bound \TYP{Object}.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex},
lines 49--50:
\begin{quote}
If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'' clause.
\end{quote}

(* IntMap's UPLUS of two many-entry maps throws KeyOverlap on a shared key in either order, and holds every entry of both where they share none. *)
component IntMapUplusManyEntry
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

overlap(f: () -> IntMap[\ZZ32\]): String = do
    msg: String := "no exception"
    try
        ignore(f())
    catch e
        UncheckedException => msg := e.asString
    end
    msg
  end

(* The two maps below share the keys 3 and 6; either may be met first. *)
sharedKey(msg: String): Boolean =
    (msg = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 3 |-> 53 and |-> 1") OR (msg = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 3 |-> 1 and |-> 53") OR
    (msg = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 6 |-> 56 and |-> 2") OR (msg = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 6 |-> 2 and |-> 56")

run(): () = do
    thirds = {[\ZZ32\] widen(3 k) |-> k | k <- 0#6}
    middle = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> 50 + k | k <- 2#6}
    assert(sharedKey(overlap(fn () => middle UPLUS thirds)), true, "keys 2 to 7 UPLUS keys 0, 3, ..., 15 throws KeyOverlap on a shared key")
    assert(sharedKey(overlap(fn () => thirds UPLUS middle)), true, "keys 0, 3, ..., 15 UPLUS keys 2 to 7 throws KeyOverlap on a shared key")
    others = {[\ZZ32\] widen(3 k + 1) |-> 100 + k | k <- 0#6}
    both = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k MOD 3 = 0 then k DIV 3 else 100 + k DIV 3 end) | k <- 0#17, k MOD 3 =/= 2}
    assert(thirds UPLUS others, both, "keys 0, 3, ..., 15 UPLUS keys 1, 4, ..., 16 holds every entry of both")
    assert(others UPLUS thirds, both, "keys 1, 4, ..., 16 UPLUS keys 0, 3, ..., 15 holds every entry of both")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

(* An IntMap comprehension or map expression whose key repeats with a different value throws KeyOverlap, whatever the order of its entries. *)
component IntMapComprehensionRepeatedKey
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

overlap(f: () -> IntMap[\ZZ32\]): String = do
    msg: String := "no exception"
    try
        ignore(f())
    catch e
        UncheckedException => msg := e.asString
    end
    msg
  end

run(): () = do
    (* keys 0, 1, 2, 0 with the values 0, 1, 2, 3 *)
    m4 = overlap(fn () => {[\ZZ32\] widen(k MOD 3) |-> k | k <- 0#4})
    assert((m4 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 0 and |-> 3") OR (m4 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 3 and |-> 0"), true,
           "a map comprehension whose key 0 repeats last with a different value throws KeyOverlap (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    (* keys 0, 1, 0, 1 with the values 0, 1, 2, 3 *)
    m2 = overlap(fn () => {[\ZZ32\] widen(k MOD 2) |-> k | k <- 0#4})
    assert((m2 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 0 and |-> 2") OR (m2 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 2 and |-> 0") OR
           (m2 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 1 |-> 1 and |-> 3") OR (m2 = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 1 |-> 3 and |-> 1"), true,
           "a map comprehension whose keys 0 and 1 each repeat with a different value throws KeyOverlap (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    ml = overlap(fn () => {[\ZZ32\] widen(0) |-> 0, widen(1) |-> 1, widen(2) |-> 2, widen(0) |-> 3})
    assert((ml = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 0 and |-> 3") OR (ml = "IntMap.KeyOverlap: 0 |-> 3 and |-> 0"), true,
           "a map expression whose key 0 repeats last with a different value throws KeyOverlap")
    distinct = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#4}
    assert(|distinct|, 4, "a map comprehension whose keys are distinct holds one entry for each key")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\revision{revival-overloading}{Done: declarations of one name may have different
static parameters, under the rules of \secref{overloading-static-params}.
Jan's pair is still not a valid overloading, since the two declarations have the
same parameter type, each applicable to every call to which the other is, which
the No Duplicates Rule refuses; \library\ write it
as one factory, \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()},
which chooses its result by a \KWD{typecase} on its type argument, a
\TYP{Vector} where the argument is a \TYP{Number}.}
\item Overloaded functionals with different \KWD{throws} clauses
----
adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
example.
A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
every call to which the other is applicable, with a box, and the box on Jan's
example in the internal document gives that rule as its reason.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
----
ignored in the remainder of this chapter.

lines 455--459, 522--524 and 567--570 of
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, and the new
section have no counterpart there.
The new section, the revival's text of 30~September 2026, stated:
\begin{quote}
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\end{quote}
and the box on Jan's example in the internal document gave as its reason that
the two declarations have the same parameter type ``and each is more specific
than the other''.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, except that the existential reduction
uses the rule of \secref{revival-routec} in place of instantiation exclusion;
the No Duplicates Rule does not depend on the rule on instantiations.
\end{description}
